content: Scalpels and electrosurgery are both viable tools for creating abdominal incisions during major surgeries. Electrosurgery offers potential advantages, such as reduced blood loss, quicker and drier tissue separation, and a lower risk of accidental injury to the surgeon. However, it may also carry risks, including delayed wound healing and a higher likelihood of surgical site infections. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of electrosurgery and scalpel use for major abdominal incisions. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated these two methods in various surgical settings, including both elective and emergency procedures. The incisions studied could be vertical, oblique, or transverse, and the layers of the abdominal wall involved included the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and musculoaponeurosis. The primary outcomes assessed were wound infection, time to wound healing, and wound dehiscence. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain, incision time, blood loss, and scar or adhesion formation. The updated review incorporated seven additional RCTs, bringing the total to 16 studies with 2769 participants. Eleven studies, involving 2178 participants, reported on wound infections. The results showed no significant difference in wound infection rates between electrosurgery (7.7%) and scalpel (7.4%) use (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.54). However, the evidence was of low certainty due to concerns about bias and imprecision. None of the studies provided data on the time required for wound healing. Regarding wound dehiscence, the evidence was very uncertain. The rates were 2.7% for electrosurgery and 2.4% for scalpel use (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.50; 1064 participants; 6 studies). This evidence was downgraded to very low certainty due to significant bias and imprecision. The time required to make an incision did not differ significantly between the two methods. Electrosurgery was slightly faster, with a mean difference of -45.74 seconds (95% CI -88.41 to -3.07; 325 participants; 4 studies). However, this evidence was of moderate certainty due to imprecision. Similarly, there was no significant difference in incision time per wound area (MD -0.58 seconds/cm², 95% CI -1.26 to 0.09; 282 participants; 3 studies), but the evidence was of low certainty due to very serious imprecision. Blood loss during surgery was also comparable between the two methods. Electrosurgery resulted in slightly less mean blood loss (MD -20.10 mL, 95% CI -28.16 to -12.05; 241 participants; 3 studies), but this evidence was of moderate certainty due to imprecision. Two studies reported on blood loss per wound area, but the data could not be pooled due to significant heterogeneity, leaving uncertainty about the effect of electrosurgery on wound-related blood loss per area. The review could not draw definitive conclusions about postoperative pain or scar appearance due to the limited number of studies, insufficient data, conflicting results, and variability in measurement methods. In conclusion, the evidence comparing electrosurgery and scalpel use for major abdominal incisions is of moderate to very low certainty. Current data suggest no clear difference in wound infection rates between the two methods. Further high-quality research is needed to better understand the relative effectiveness and safety of these techniques.
